figures.caption: Figure 1: Neural-state segmentation and reusable computation. (A) GSBS constructs state templates, searches candidate boundaries and selects the state count using t-distance. (B) Temporal prefixes supply reusable interval scores, Qa,b = F (a, b); single and double splits replace only their parent contribution. The best proposals undergo t-distance comparison and sequential refinement. (C) Two-dimensional prefixes of valid-pair counts, correlations and squared correlations provide within-state and adjacent-state statistics by four-corner queries. The full symmetric correlation matrix is shown; statistics use each eligible pair once. Three numerical backends feed a shared search controller. Data-derived elements use a 120-TR Sherlock fMRI excerpt [5, 6]; heatmaps show feature subsets, while fitting uses all 4,230 voxels. Detailed construction and provenance are in Supplementary Section S4.

Figure 2: Segmentation agreement on a four-state signal. (A) Synthetic activity; dashed lines mark generating boundaries. (B) Ground truth and selected boundaries from the official implementation and three HP-GSBS backends. (C) Complete t-distance curves, retaining double-insertion indexing; all routes select K = 4. (D) Absolute differences from official values; GPU curves overlap. Seed 19; noise standard deviation 0.05; T = 80, P = 16, Kmax = 12.

Figure 3: Real EEG segmentation from saved full-record fits. (A) Standardized 64-channel EEG and the selected state sequence; alternating colours distinguish adjacent intervals. (B) A fixed central window (120.51–140.43 s), with boundaries from four implementations aligned beneath the input. Both EEG heatmaps use a colour scale clipped at ±3. (C) Full symmetric spatial-pattern correlations for the same window; outlined blocks mark selected state intervals. (D) All evaluated t-distance indices, preserving double-insertion indexing; marker positions are staggered for visibility. All routes select 126 states with identical boundary histories and a maximum absolute TD difference of 2.43 × 10−13. Parameters: Kmax = 131, dmin=5, statewise detection, sequential refinement, block size 50 and FP64.

Figure 4: Controlled complete-fit performance. (A–C) Runtime versus T , P and Kmax, with the other two fixed. Small filled points show two per-input observations; open markers show their median, and whiskers their range. HP observations summarize three timed fits after warm-up; official observations are single fits. The annotation in B gives central-configuration runtimes. (D–F) Same-input official/HP speedups across seeds; D highlights the median PyTorch speedup at T = 768. The central configuration is reused across panels. All fits use statewise detection and sequential refinement.

Figure 5: Computation reuse, memory and parallel execution. (A) CPU ablation on a 1336 × 64 EEG input, Kmax = 131. (B) Left: peak process RSS and complete-fit time for a 5000 × 8 input. Right: four increasing low-memory workloads; both T and P change. Separate measurements give 190.6 and 191.1 MiB at 5000 × 8. All B measurements use single-boundary search, no refinement, block size zero and Kmax = 16. (C,D) Throughput versus CPU workers and GPU batch size for short synthetic and high-K EEG inputs. CPU batches contain 32 and eight tasks, respectively; high-K tasks repeat one EEG input. A, B runtimes and C/D show three-run medians and observed-range whiskers; memory values are measured peaks. These are existing release-development measurements.
